chunks: And from him, from Abd al-Rahman, from Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who passed the time when people enter the state of Ihram, but he forgot or was unaware, so he did not enter Ihram until he arrived at Mecca. He feared that if he returned to the Miqat, the Hajj would be missed for him. He said: 'He exits from the Haram (sanctuary) and enters Ihram, and that will suffice for him.'

And there is no contradiction between this narration and the first one, because he is only obliged to exit from the Haram if he does not fear that by exiting, the Hajj will be missed for him. Just as if he does not fear missing the Hajj by exiting to the Miqat of his people, it is obligatory for him to go to it. And there is no harm for the one compelled and fearing for his life to delay entering Ihram from the Miqat until he enters the Haram. This was narrated.

key_terms.الْإِحْرَام: Ihram (the sacred state of consecration for Hajj or Umrah)
key_terms.الْمُضْطَرّ: Al-Mudtar (one who is compelled or under duress)
key_terms.الْمِيقَات: Miqat (the designated boundary or place where pilgrims enter the state of Ihram)
key_terms.فَوْتَ الْحَجِّ: Fawt al-Hajj (missing or losing the Hajj opportunity)

ai.seo_question: What should a pilgrim do if they miss the Miqat and enter Mecca without entering Ihram?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction between this narration and the preceding one by distinguishing between the general obligation to return to the Miqat and the exception for those who fear missing the Hajj season if they do so. This ruling highlights the Shia principle of *al-makhafah* (fear of loss) as a valid legal excuse (*rukhsah*) that permits entering Ihram within the Haram boundaries, ensuring the validity of the pilgrimage without undue hardship.
